subChunks.title: Classes & Objects

storyBeats.text: Eldrin unrolls an enormous parchment labelled Wizard Blueprint. It shows fields for name, level, and school — but the parchment itself is not a wizard.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The class is the blueprint. The object is what you build from it. You build me — Archmage Eldrin — from the Wizard blueprint. You could build a hundred wizards from the same blueprint; each one is distinct.

storyBeats.label: Blueprint and instances

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The new keyword is the incantation that brings the blueprint to life. It allocates memory and returns a reference to the newly created object.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a class Spell with fields String name and int power, and a method describe() that prints "[name] deals [power] damage". Create two Spell objects and call describe() on each.
guidedPractice.hint: Define the Spell class inside ClassBasics, create two instances with different name/power values.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the relationship between a class and an object in Java using an analogy from everyday life.

questions.prompt: What keyword is used to create a new object from a class in Java?
questions.explanation: The new keyword allocates memory for the object and calls its constructor.

questions.prompt: Changing a field on one object affects all other objects created from the same class.
questions.explanation: Each object has its own independent copy of its instance fields. Changing one object's field has no effect on others (unless the field is static).
The name field is set to "Rex" before bark() is called, so it prints "Rex says Woof!"

subChunks.title: Constructors & the this Keyword

storyBeats.text: Eldrin taps the Wizard blueprint. Below the fields, a section reads Initialisation Ritual.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every well-made object is initialised at the moment of creation. The constructor is that ritual. You provide the ingredients — name and level — and the object emerges fully formed, ready to use.

storyBeats.label: Constructor in action

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice this.name = name. The this on the left refers to the field; the plain name on the right is the parameter. Without this, the field would never be set.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a class Potion with fields String type and int strength, and a constructor that takes both. Add a method use() that prints "Used [type] potion (+[strength] HP)". Create and use two potions.
guidedPractice.hint: Remember to use 'this.type = type' in the constructor to distinguish the field from the parameter.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is a constructor in Java? Why do we use 'this' inside constructors, and what happens if you forget it?

questions.prompt: What does the this keyword refer to inside a method or constructor?
questions.explanation: this is a reference to the object on which the method or constructor was invoked.

options: The constructor has no return type
String fields cannot be set in constructors
questions.explanation: Without this, both sides refer to the local parameter. The field name is never assigned. Use this.name = name to distinguish field from parameter.

questions.prompt: If you define a parameterised constructor in a Java class, Java still provides the no-argument constructor automatically.
questions.explanation: Once you define any constructor, Java stops providing the default no-arg constructor. If you need both, define both explicitly.

subChunks.title: toString() and equals()

storyBeats.text: Eldrin prints two wizard scrolls. Both show Wizard@4e50df2e — completely useless information.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Java's default toString() shows a memory address — the vault room and shelf number, not the wizard's identity. Override it to tell Java how your object should introduce itself.

storyBeats.label: Meaningful toString

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And equals() — by default it checks if two variables point to the same object in memory. Override it to check if two objects represent the same value.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a Point class with int x and int y. Override toString() to return "(x, y)". Override equals() to return true when both coordinates match. Print two points and check if they are equal.
guidedPractice.hint: In equals(), cast the Object parameter to Point and compare both x and y fields.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why should you override both equals() and hashCode() together in Java? What can go wrong if you only override one?

questions.prompt: When is toString() called automatically in Java?
options: When the object is printed or concatenated with a String
When the object is compared with ==
questions.answer: When the object is printed or concatenated with a String
questions.explanation: toString() is called by System.out.println(obj) and string concatenation like "Value: " + obj.
b == b compares a reference to itself — always true. b == c compares two different objects — different memory addresses, so false.
